3. Write the rule around signals every variant must keep: the executable (Image, OriginalFileName) and short essential tokens, rather than exact spellings or long literal strings. Useful Sigma tools: |contains on short tokens, |windash for option prefixes, |re for tolerant patterns. Use logsource category: process_creation, product: windows, and give the rule a title, a description, a level and falsepositives. Describe the behavior, not these particular test commands. Some test attacks swap in look-alike characters (superscript letters such as ᵃ, small or odd dashes such as ﹣, invisible spaces). Never list those characters in the rule, and never spell out such variants letter by letter: the quality gate rejects any rule that contains them, and a real attacker will pick different ones. Instead, key on the parts no variant can change (the executable, a registry path, a short essential keyword) and use |windash for option prefixes. Do not use the |cased modifier: the rule must also run in Elastic. Never copy the specific odd characters a mutation used (invisible or look-alike Unicode) into the rule, and avoid strings that only appear in these test attacks (task names, file paths): the rule must catch variants you have not seen. Keep the delimiter on short option tokens ('/ru ', not 'ru'): a bare one- or two-letter value matches inside ordinary words and is rejected. Inside single quotes a backslash is literal, so write each regex escape once ('\bSYSTEM\b', '\s+'); a doubled '\\b' looks for a real backslash and matches nothing.
